title: Lessons From Anniversaries: October 7, Three Years On | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: CFR president Michael Froman argues that three years after October 7, Israel's wars have turned a covertly unstable Middle East into a nakedly unstable one: Iran and its proxies are heavily degraded, but Israel has spent down international goodwill and Iran has shown asymmetric leverage over the global economy. Drawing parallels with post-9/11 U.S. wars, he urges Israel and the U.S. to plan Gaza's long-term future, with the Board of Peace's $2.4 billion project slate as a test case.

themes.theme: Region shifted from covert to open instability

insights.claim: Three years of war since October 7, 2023 have transformed the Middle East from covertly unstable to nakedly unstable, with proxy conflicts becoming direct conflicts and espionage replaced by air strikes and ground invasions.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Higher baseline of overt state-on-state conflict implies a persistently elevated geopolitical risk premium for the region.
insights.quote: have transformed a region that was covertly unstable into one that is now nakedly so

insights.claim: After tolerating decades of low-intensity conflict, Israel treated October 7 as a permission structure to address regional adversaries comprehensively and permanently, including Gaza, Lebanon and, with the U.S., Iran in the Twelve Day War and a later U.S. 'excursion'.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Israeli strategic doctrine has shifted from containment to elimination, raising escalation propensity.
insights.quote: Israel decided that October 7 created a permission structure to address its regional adversaries more comprehensively and permanently

insights.claim: Before October 7, Hezbollah had 120,000 precision rockets able to hit critical infrastructure across Israel, Syria hosted Russian bases and IRGC deployments supplying Hezbollah, and Iran had domestic nuclear infrastructure plus proxies in Gaza, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen; almost all of that has changed.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Iran's 'axis' network has been structurally dismantled, reducing some tail risks to Israeli infrastructure.

insights.claim: Hamas and Hezbollah are now a shadow of their former selves, Iran's nuclear program lies under rubble and its navy is largely destroyed, and Syria has a new government working closely with the U.S. and seeking a modus vivendi with Israel.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Regional realignment (Syria toward the U.S.) opens possible reconstruction and normalization opportunities.

insights.claim: Israel's Lebanon campaign degraded Hezbollah and gave Lebanon a chance to restore sovereignty and self-rule, while Israel has kept relations with all Abraham Accords countries.

insights.so_what: Lebanon state-rebuilding and Abraham Accords durability are upside scenarios to monitor.

insights.claim: Iran has shown that even with degraded military capabilities it and its proxies need little to wreak havoc and gain leverage over the global economy through asymmetric warfare.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Military defeat of Iran does not remove its ability to disrupt global trade and energy flows; keep shipping/energy risk premia in mind.

insights.claim: Drawing on U.S. Middle East wars, Froman argues great powers are frustrated not by losing wars but by spending down international goodwill and strategic advantages; such wars end in exhaustion and hopelessness rather than a Versailles-style settlement.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Expect a protracted, unresolved conflict rather than a clean peace settlement.
insights.quote: Wars like this don’t tend to end at Versailles. They end with exhaustion and hopelessness.

insights.claim: Froman sees Israel's post-October 7 trajectory as eerily similar to the U.S. after 9/11: hazy intelligence, fog of war and mission creep drawing a powerful country into a quagmire with broad security, political and global-standing implications; the last U.S. troops left Iraq this week.

insights.so_what: Quagmire risk implies long-duration costs for Israel's economy, politics and alliances.

insights.claim: Israel and the U.S. need to begin a serious conversation on Gaza's long-term future and the limits of nation-building, with the U.S. able to share lessons from reforming nations previously run by dictators and warlords.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Postwar Gaza governance planning remains unresolved, a key uncertainty for reconstruction.

insights.claim: The Trump-proposed, UN Security Council-endorsed Board of Peace, though imperfect, may be a rare opportunity absent credible alternatives; last week it proposed $2.4 billion in projects, including winterizing structures in Gaza, with success depending on implementation.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
